newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey welcomes ousted Afghan warlord Dostum.
newsitem.headline: Turkey welcomes ousted Afghan warlord Dostum.

text.p: Turkey said on Monday that ousted Afghan general, Abdul Rashid Dostum, who arrived in Ankara on Sunday, could stay as long as he wanted.
Dostum was toppled from his fiefdom in northern Afghanistan at the weekend by fighters allied to the Islamic Taleban movement.
"He is welcome in Turkey...Of course the length of his stay in Turkey depends on his own wishes," Turkish foreign ministry spokesman Omer Akbel told a news briefing.

Dostum's private plane landed in the Turkish capital early on Sunday from his headquarters in the northern Afghan town of Mazar-i-Sharif, which fell to his former commander General Abdul Malik in a mutiny last week.

He said he had come to Ankara for health reasons and was not planning to seek political asylum in the country. "Our only request from Turkey is that it takes the lead to bring war to an end in Afghanistan," Dostum said.
He vowed to continue to struggle for control of Afghanistan.
"I have been struggling for Afghanistan for 20 years and this struggle will continue," Dostum said.
Akbel said Turkey has constant contacts with other countries concerned about Afghanistan, but gave no more details.
"We would like to have a broad-based peace and stability in Afghanistan," he said.
Pakistan on Sunday became the first country to recognise the Taleban as the legitimate rulers of neighbouring Afghanistan and urged other countries and organisations to do the same.

General Abdul Malik's mutiny against Dostum has, for the moment at least, ended opposition for the Taleban in the Uzbek-dominated parts of the northern plains and opened the way to the collapse of anti-Taleban opposition alliance.
Ankara has so far not had any contacts with the Taleban and has closed down its diplomatic premises in Afghanistan, Akbel said.

Turkey was widely reported to have supported the ethnic Uzbek leader Dostum, along with Uzbekistan. Turks and Uzbeks share common ethnic and linguistic links. The secular Turkish establishment has previously expressed concern about the purist Islamist nature of Taleban.
